aj.protect.summary: Arcjet rate limiting limits how many requests a client can make during a time period. It can identify clients by IP address or by custom values such as a user ID.
aj.protect.explanation: aj.protect executes the configured Arcjet rules for a request and returns an ArcjetDecision. A rate-limit rule counts requests using its configured algorithm and characteristics. If the decision is denied, the handler can return an HTTP error such as 429.

parameters.name: characteristics
parameters.description: Values for configured custom characteristics, such as a user ID.

parameters.name: requested
parameters.description: The number of tokens to remove for a token bucket rule.

interview.question: How does a rate limit identify a client?
interview.answer: Use characteristics to choose how Arcjet identifies a client. The default characteristic is the client IP address. You can pass values such as a user ID to protect each user separately.
interview.followUp: How can anonymous and logged-in users use different identifiers? Create augmented clients with withRule or with_rule so each client uses its own characteristics.

interview.question: How does a token bucket request specify usage?
interview.answer: A token bucket rule requires the request to specify how many tokens to remove. The requested value must be a positive integer.
interview.followUp: What happens if a request asks for more tokens than are available? The rule can deny the request because the bucket cannot satisfy the withdrawal.

interview.question: What are the tradeoffs between middleware and route-level rate limits?
interview.answer: Arcjet can run a rule in middleware or in a route handler. Middleware is useful for broad coverage, while a route handler keeps the rule beside the protected code and provides route-specific context.
interview.followUp: What should you check when both locations are used? Make sure the same request does not reach Arcjet twice, usually by excluding the route from the middleware matcher.

keyPoints: Characteristics decide which requests share one rate-limit counter.
If you provide no custom characteristic, Arcjet uses the client IP address.
Custom characteristic values may be strings, numbers, or booleans.
Token bucket calls use requested to state how many tokens the request consumes.
requested must be a positive integer.
A route-level rule applies to that route, while middleware can cover selected paths or broader traffic.
gotchas: Do not use an email address as a rate-limit characteristic. Use a non-sensitive identifier instead.
Run Arcjet once per request. Exclude route handlers from the middleware matcher when they already apply Arcjet.
Exclude health and liveness probe routes because these requests may lack metadata needed for security decisions.

interview.question: What does withRule do?
interview.answer: withRule adds an ad-hoc rule to an existing Arcjet client and returns another client. You can call it more than once to add multiple rules, then call protect on the result.
interview.followUp: Why reuse the base client? The SDK caches decisions and configuration, so one shared instance avoids creating a new client for every request.

interview.question: When should you use an ad-hoc rule?
interview.answer: It is useful when a rule depends on handler logic, such as applying rate limiting only to users who are not authenticated. The base rules and configuration remain available on the returned client.
interview.followUp: How would you apply two conditional protections? Chain two withRule calls on the selected client, as shown in the Node.js reference.

interview.question: What can withRule accept and return?
interview.answer: withRule accepts a rule object created by a rule helper, such as fixedWindow or detectBot. The returned client exposes protect, which produces a decision that can be checked with isDenied().
interview.followUp: How should a denied rate-limit decision be reported? Return HTTP status 429; other denied decisions can use HTTP status 403.

The result is a client. Call its protect method to evaluate a request.

allow.sourceTitle: Sensitive information reference for Python + FastAPI
allow.summary: Python + FastAPI sensitive information detection checks request text for entities such as email addresses, names, addresses, and identifiers. Configure an allow or deny list and use Rampart for local detection.
allow.explanation: The rule checks text passed as sensitive_info_value. In LIVE mode, a denied entity blocks the request. In DRY_RUN mode, Arcjet records the result without blocking. Use either allow or deny, not both. The Rampart backend performs detection locally.
allow.syntax: def detect_sensitive_info(*, mode: Mode, allow: Sequence[str | SensitiveInfoEntityType] = (), deny: Sequence[str | SensitiveInfoEntityType] = (), backend: SensitiveInfoBackend = ...) -> SensitiveInfoDetection

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: Controls whether the rule blocks requests or only logs results.

parameters.name: allow
parameters.description: Entity types to permit; mutually exclusive with deny.

parameters.name: deny
parameters.description: Entity types to block; mutually exclusive with allow.

parameters.name: backend
parameters.description: Detection backend, such as the Rampart backend.

example.title: Deny email addresses
example.code:
from arcjet import Mode, arcjet, detect_sensitive_info, SensitiveInfoEntityType
from arcjet_sensitive_info_rampart import rampart

aj = arcjet(
    key="ARCJET_KEY",
    rules=[detect_sensitive_info(
        mode=Mode.LIVE,
        deny=[SensitiveInfoEntityType.EMAIL],
        backend=rampart(),
    )],
)
example.explanation: This rule denies requests containing detected email addresses.

interview.question: How do you configure sensitive information detection in Python?
interview.answer: Use detect_sensitive_info with Mode.LIVE, then provide either an allow list or a deny list. Pass the resulting rule to the Arcjet client and scan request text with sensitive_info_value.
interview.followUp: How would you test it safely? Use Mode.DRY_RUN first and inspect the rule results before switching to LIVE.

interview.question: How does the Rampart backend detect sensitive information?
interview.answer: Rampart runs the NER model on the device and also uses deterministic recognizers for structured values. Python uses the sensitive-info-rampart package and passes rampart() as the backend.
interview.followUp: What happens when both methods match? The deterministic recognizer takes precedence over the model.

interview.question: What happens if sensitive information processing fails?
interview.answer: Arcjet normally fails open and returns an ERROR result for a rule when processing fails. The error result includes a message, so applications can log it or choose to reject the request themselves.
interview.followUp: What is the default timeout? Arcjet fails open after 2000 milliseconds by default.

keyPoints: An allow list permits only the listed entity types. Other detected types are denied.
A deny list blocks only the listed entity types. Other detected types are allowed.
Python accepts enum members or string names such as SensitiveInfoEntityType.EMAIL and GIVEN_NAME.
Rampart covers named entities, address parts, and government or financial identifiers.
A validated recognizer has priority when it and the model identify the same text.
The rule can be exercised locally and in continuous integration without a different runtime setup.
gotchas: Do not pass allow and deny together.
Use DRY_RUN when testing so requests are not blocked.
A timeout normally allows the request. Handle ERROR results if your route needs fail-closed behavior.
Phone numbers are detected by the model, not by the default structured recognizer.

Allow free email.explanation: Arcjet first checks the address format locally in the SDK. The check follows several RFC rules but excludes patterns that are usually unsuitable for real application sign-ups, such as local domains. You can configure whether the domain must contain two parts and whether domain literals are accepted.

useCases.scenario: Apply application-specific rules to domain formatting.

interview.question: Where does the initial email validation run?
interview.answer: The SDK checks syntax locally before any other email checks. It uses several RFCs, with changes that exclude addresses such as local domains.
interview.followUp: What syntax settings can be changed? You can control whether the domain needs two parts and whether domain literals are permitted.

interview.question: What are the configurable validation options?
interview.answer: The default requires two domain parts. The default also rejects domain literals, such as an address using an IP address in brackets.
interview.followUp: Why might an application change these defaults? A specialized application may need to accept a narrower or broader set of valid address formats.

interview.question: Why use email validation during sign-up?
interview.answer: Email validation helps reject malformed or unsuitable addresses before sign-up. Arcjet also describes email verification as a separate capability for preventing fake accounts and reducing spam or fraud.
interview.followUp: Does syntax validation prove mailbox ownership? No. Ownership requires a separate verification step, such as sending a confirmation message.

keyPoints: The first syntax check runs locally in the SDK.
The rules follow several RFCs but remove formats that are poor fits for normal application sign-ups.
Local-only domains are excluded by the validation rules.
The documentation exposes two configurable validation settings.
One setting controls whether the domain must have two parts.
The other setting controls acceptance of bracketed IP address domains.

allowBots.explanation: `allowBots` is an Arcjet bot-protection configuration that uses an allow list. Detected bots named in the list can pass; detected bots not named in the list are denied. The allow and deny forms cannot be used together.

parameters.description: Optional enforcement mode. Use `LIVE` or `DRY_RUN`.

parameters.description: Bots or bot categories to allow. Detected bots not listed are denied.

example.explanation: This rule allows detected search-engine bots and blocks other detected bots.

useCases.scenario: Allow search engines to crawl public pages while blocking other detected bots.

useCases.title: Policy testing

interview.question: How does an allow list affect detected bots?
interview.answer: `allowBots` configures bot detection with an allow list. Arcjet permits detected bots that match the list and denies detected bots that do not match it.
interview.followUp: What happens with an empty allow list? It is valid and blocks every detected bot.

interview.question: Can a rule define both allow and deny?
interview.answer: The bot configuration must contain exactly one of `allow` or `deny`. These two lists are mutually exclusive.
interview.followUp: Why is this restriction useful? It prevents an ambiguous policy where the same rule both allows and denies selected bots.

interview.question: What other option can be set on the bot rule?
interview.answer: The optional `mode` can be `LIVE` or `DRY_RUN`. The configuration also accepts well-known bots and bot categories in its allow list.
interview.followUp: How would you test a policy without enforcing it? Set `mode` to `DRY_RUN`, then review the resulting decisions before switching to `LIVE`.

keyPoints: The rule can use an allow policy or a deny policy for selected bots.
An allow policy blocks detected bots that are missing from the list.
A deny policy permits detected bots unless they are listed.
The configuration cannot combine allow and deny lists.
The rule can run in live enforcement mode or dry-run mode.
gotchas: Use either `allow` or `deny`, but not both and not neither.
An empty allow list blocks all detected bots.
An allow list is not an allow-by-default setting for unknown bots.

ArcjetDecision.summary: ArcjetDecision is the result returned by protect after Arcjet evaluates the configured rules for a request. It gives the final conclusion, rule details, request ID, TTL, reason, and client IP analysis.
ArcjetDecision.explanation: Call protect with the incoming request. It returns a promise for an ArcjetDecision. Inspect its conclusion with methods such as isAllowed, isDenied, or isErrored. The decision also contains the rule results, reason, time-to-live, request ID, and client IP analysis.

parameters.name: request
parameters.description: The incoming framework request object used to evaluate the configured rules.

parameters.name: props
parameters.description: Additional rule data, such as userId or email, when a configured rule requires it.

ArcjetDecision.returns: A Promise that resolves to an ArcjetDecision.

example.explanation: Create a decision by passing the request to protect, then reject the request when isDenied returns true.

useCases.scenario: A Next.js route needs to allow or reject an incoming request after security rules run.

useCases.title: Inspect rule results
useCases.scenario: A developer needs to learn which configured rule affected a request.

useCases.title: Read IP information
useCases.scenario: An application needs request location details from Arcjet's IP analysis.

interview.question: How do you use ArcjetDecision?
interview.answer: Call await aj.protect(request) and inspect the returned ArcjetDecision. Use isDenied to reject a request, isAllowed to accept it, and isErrored to detect an unrecoverable error.
interview.followUp: How do you inspect which rule caused the result? Iterate over decision.results and inspect each rule result's conclusion and reason.

interview.question: How is the final conclusion selected?
interview.answer: The overall conclusion uses the highest severity from all configured rules. DENY is strongest, followed by CHALLENGE, ERROR, and ALLOW.
interview.followUp: What if one rule errors but another denies? The overall conclusion is DENY, while the error can be inspected in the individual results.

interview.question: What information is in decision.results?
interview.answer: Each configured rule produces an ArcjetRuleResult when evaluated. Its state shows whether it ran, ran in dry-run mode, was skipped, or used a cached denial.
interview.followUp: Why might a rule be NOT_RUN? An earlier rule may already have produced a conclusion that applies to the request.

keyPoints: Pass the incoming handler request to protect.
The decision ID identifies the request and can be used to find it in the Arcjet dashboard.
ttl tells you how many seconds the decision remains valid.
Use results to examine each configured rule separately.
isDenied returns true when Arcjet rejects the request.
The ip field contains Arcjet's client IP analysis, including location data when available.
gotchas: protect is asynchronous, so await its returned promise before checking the decision.
Use an ESM project. CommonJS is not supported.
A denied result may be cached until its TTL expires, so later requests may not run every rule again.

The decision reason represents the highest-priority rule that produced the final conclusion; inspect decision.results to examine every rule.

interview.question: What is ArcjetReason used for?
interview.answer: ArcjetReason contains details about the rule behind a decision conclusion. Its type-checking methods can identify rules such as bot protection, rate limiting, and prompt injection.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect all rule outcomes? Iterate over decision.results and inspect each result.reason separately.

interview.question: Does the decision reason include every configured rule?
interview.answer: The decision-level reason is the highest-priority rule that produced the final conclusion. Other rule outcomes are available in the results array.
interview.followUp: Why might the decision reason differ from a rule that returned an error? A higher-severity conclusion, such as DENY, takes priority over ERROR.

interview.question: Why must code check the reason type before reading its fields?
interview.answer: Rule-specific reason data depends on the rule type. For example, bot protection has allowed and denied bot arrays, while rate limiting has max, remaining, window, and reset values.
interview.followUp: How should code safely read these fields? First use the matching reason check, then access that rule type's properties.

keyPoints: A decision has a reason object that explains the final conclusion in more detail.
Use decision.results to inspect rule outcomes beyond the final decision reason.
Bot protection reasons list the identifiers of allowed and denied bots.
Rate-limit reasons expose max, remaining, window, and reset values.

interview.question: How do you protect a React Router request?
interview.answer: Call arcjet.protect with the route loader arguments and any extra properties required by the configured rules. It returns a promise, so await it and inspect the decision, commonly with isDenied().
interview.followUp: What should happen when protect returns an error? Arcjet is designed to fail open; inspect reason.message and log the problem rather than automatically blocking the request.

interview.question: How is the final decision calculated?
interview.answer: The overall result is DENY if any LIVE rule denies. If no LIVE rule denies but one returns ERROR, the overall result is ERROR; otherwise it is ALLOW. DRY_RUN results are reported but do not change the overall result.
interview.followUp: Can a DRY_RUN rule block a request? No. Its result appears in results, but it does not affect the top-level conclusion.

interview.question: What is required when creating the client?
interview.answer: The client requires key and rules. The key identifies the Arcjet site, and rules define the checks that protect requests. The key is usually supplied from process.env.ARCJET_KEY.
interview.followUp: Why reuse one client? The SDK caches decisions and configuration, so one shared instance avoids repeated setup and improves performance.

keyPoints: The package requires React Router 7 or newer and Node.js 22.21.0 or newer, or a similar ESM runtime.
The key identifies the site in Arcjet. The client also needs an array of rules.
protect is asynchronous. Await its promise before checking the decision.
When Arcjet calls its Cloud API, the decision can include IP location and reputation details.
gotchas: Do not expect the SDK to read ARCJET_KEY by itself. Read it from the environment and pass it as the key option.
Do not create the client for every request. Reuse a client created outside the handler.
An error may allow the request. Log error details when needed instead of treating every error as a denial.

interview.question: How do allow and deny differ?
interview.answer: A bot rule uses either allow or deny. With allow, only listed detected bots are accepted; with deny, listed bots are blocked and other detected bots are allowed.
interview.followUp: What does an empty allow list do? It blocks every detected bot.

interview.question: How do you handle a denied bot request?
interview.answer: Use protect with the request context. Inspect the returned decision with isDenied() and reason.isBot() to identify a bot denial.
interview.followUp: What information else is available? The decision includes an ID, conclusion, reason, rule results, and IP details.

interview.question: How are bots identified?
interview.answer: Arcjet identifies more than 600 bots and groups them into 23 categories. Rules can name an individual bot, such as CURL, or a category, such as CATEGORY:AI.
interview.followUp: How does advanced detection improve identification? It adds IP reputation, verification, machine learning, and other signals.

keyPoints: Arcjet can recognize over 600 known bots.
Known bots are grouped into 23 categories, which you can use in rules.
Rules can target one bot or a whole category.
Client tracking uses configurable fingerprints, with the IP address as the default.
In-app rules can use request context such as identity, subscription, and business logic.

interview.question: How does AI budget control work?
interview.answer: Configure a token bucket with a characteristic such as userId, a refill rate, an interval, and a capacity. Call Protect with WithRequested to charge the estimated token count, then reject denied decisions.
interview.followUp: How would you support paid plans? Calculate refill and capacity from the user's subscription level, then pass those values to the rule.

interview.question: What do the token bucket settings control?
interview.answer: The characteristic creates a separate bucket for each user. RefillRate and Interval define the sustained allowance, while Capacity limits the largest burst that can accumulate.
interview.followUp: Why keep capacity separate from refill rate? Capacity permits short bursts without changing the user's long-term average allowance.

interview.question: How should a handler enforce the limit?
interview.answer: Estimate the request's token use, pass it through WithRequested, and check IsDenied. A denied request should return an HTTP 429 response instead of calling the AI provider.
interview.followUp: What happens if token use is underestimated? The user can consume more provider budget than the rule reserved, so estimates should be conservative or based on measured usage.

keyPoints: Token buckets fit token-based AI billing because requests consume variable amounts of tokens.
Refilling provides a continuing allowance instead of resetting all usage at one sharp boundary.
For example, a rate of 2,000 and a one-hour interval gives each user's bucket 2,000 tokens per hour.
Capacity sets the upper limit of saved tokens and therefore controls the largest permitted burst.
Fixed-window and sliding-window rules are alternatives when a hard daily, weekly, or monthly cap is preferred.
gotchas: The request must include its estimated token cost with WithRequested. A poor estimate can make the budget inaccurate.
Use a characteristic that truly identifies one user, such as an authenticated ID, API key, or session token.
The shown refill values are examples. Subscription plans or other factors can provide different values.

interview.question: How is `CREDIT_CARD_NUMBER` detected?
interview.answer: `CREDIT_CARD_NUMBER` is detected by a deterministic recognizer. It validates the digit pattern and requires a valid Luhn check digit.
interview.followUp: Why use a recognizer instead of only the model? The recognizer gives deterministic validation for structured values such as card numbers.

interview.question: What input does sensitive-information detection scan?
interview.answer: Pass the text to `sensitiveInfoValue` when calling `protect`. For a request endpoint, this can be the request body or another selected value.
interview.followUp: How would you scan all chat messages? Pass the complete conversation history instead of only the newest message.

interview.question: What is the difference between `allow` and `deny`?
interview.answer: Use `deny` to block listed entity types and allow other detected types. Use `allow` to block detected types that are not listed.
interview.followUp: How can detection be tested without blocking? Set the rule mode to `DRY_RUN`, which logs detections without rejecting requests.

keyPoints: Use `allow` when only named entity types are acceptable. Use `deny` when only selected types must be blocked.
`CREDIT_CARD_NUMBER` uses a validated pattern, unlike model-only entities such as names.
Formatted card numbers with spaces or dashes are still checked.
When both detection methods identify the same text, the deterministic recognizer takes priority.
The documentation gives several valid card-number examples, including grouped and dashed forms.
Detection uses the local Rampart backend and does not require sending request content to a remote service.
gotchas: A card number must have 13–19 digits and pass the Luhn check. Spaces and dashes are ignored.
Configure either `allow` or `deny`, not both.
Do not depend on the order of multiple sensitive-information rules.

interview.question: How do you check an Arcjet decision?
interview.answer: Use isAllowed() when the request may continue, isDenied() when it must be rejected, and isErrored() when Arcjet reports an unrecoverable error. The overall result is based on the most severe finding among the configured rules.
interview.followUp: What happens if one rule returns an error and another denies the request? The overall conclusion is denied because DENY has higher severity than ERROR.

interview.question: How is the final conclusion selected?
interview.answer: The severity order is DENY, CHALLENGE, ERROR, then ALLOW. A higher item in this order determines the final conclusion when multiple rules run.
interview.followUp: Which result wins between CHALLENGE and ERROR? CHALLENGE wins because it has higher severity.

interview.question: What does the reason property provide?
interview.answer: The reason property gives the category of the rule that caused the final conclusion. Its methods include isBot(), isEmail(), isRateLimit(), isSensitiveInfo(), isPromptInjection(), isShield(), and isError().
interview.followUp: How can you inspect rules that did not determine the final reason? Iterate over the decision's results property.

keyPoints: isAllowed() returns true when Arcjet allows the request.
isDenied() returns true when Arcjet denies the request.
isErrored() returns true when an unrecoverable error occurred.
The severity order starts with DENY, then CHALLENGE, then ERROR, and ends with ALLOW.
The reason property contains an ArcjetReason object that describes the final rule category.
isBot() identifies a conclusion caused by bot protection.
isRateLimit() identifies a conclusion caused by an exceeded rate limit.

interview.question: How does Arcjet validate an email address?
interview.answer: Arcjet uses two stages. The SDK first checks syntax locally, then remote verification checks signals such as disposable status, MX records, and Gravatar presence. The result is used to accept, reject, or review an address.
interview.followUp: Which checks can show that an address may not be deliverable? An invalid format fails syntax validation, and a domain without MX records is treated as unable to receive email.

interview.question: How do allow and deny differ?
interview.answer: Use validateEmail with either an allow array or a deny array. A deny list rejects the listed types and allows the rest; an allow list permits only the listed types and rejects all others.
interview.followUp: What happens with allow: []? It allows no email types, so all email types are rejected.

interview.question: How can application code inspect the result?
interview.answer: The rule can report DISPOSABLE, FREE, NO_MX_RECORDS, NO_GRAVATAR, or INVALID. In JavaScript, application code can inspect decision.reason.emailTypes and use decision.isDenied() to handle a rejection.
interview.followUp: How can testing avoid blocking requests? Set the rule mode to DRY_RUN; it logs rule results without blocking requests.

interview.question: What is an Arcjet fingerprint and what is its default input?

interview.question: Which built-in characteristics can be used?

Fixed window.summary: Arcjet fixed-window rate limiting limits how many requests a client can make during a set time period. It supports live enforcement or dry-run logging and can identify clients with configured characteristics.
Fixed window.explanation: A fixed-window rule counts requests for each client during a set period. When the count reaches the maximum, live mode blocks more requests until the window ends. The client identity comes from the selected characteristics; Python uses seconds as an integer for the window.
Fixed window.syntax: fixed_window(*, mode: Mode, window: int, max: int, characteristics: Sequence[str] = ()) -> FixedWindow

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: Enforcement mode. LIVE blocks requests; DRY_RUN logs only.

parameters.name: characteristics
parameters.description: Client properties used to identify the client.

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Length of the fixed window. JavaScript/TypeScript accepts a duration string or seconds; Python accepts integer seconds.

parameters.name: max
parameters.description: Maximum requests allowed during the window.

Fixed window.returns: A fixed-window rate-limit rule: FixedWindow in Python.

example.title: Fixed window rule
example.code:
import os
from arcjet import Mode, arcjet, fixed_window

aj = arcjet(
    key=os.environ["ARCJET_KEY"],
    rules=[fixed_window(mode=Mode.LIVE, window=60, max=10)],
)
example.explanation: This creates a live rule that allows 10 requests in each 60-second window.

interview.question: How does the fixed window algorithm work?
interview.answer: fixedWindow counts a client's requests during a fixed period, such as 60 seconds. After max requests, the client is blocked until the period ends.
interview.followUp: What is the main weakness? A client can burst near the end of one period and again at the start of the next period.

interview.question: Which options configure a fixed window rule?

interview.question: When should fixedWindow be used instead of another algorithm?

interview.question: How do you add Arcjet to a Hono application?
interview.answer: Install @arcjet/node and configure an Arcjet client with ARCJET_KEY. Add rules such as Shield, bot detection, or token-bucket rate limiting, then protect incoming requests and handle denied decisions.
interview.followUp: What happens during a Cloud API outage? Cached local decisions can still work; otherwise the default is to allow the request, unless the application chooses fail-closed handling.

interview.question: What performance overhead should you expect?
interview.answer: The SDK performs work locally or asynchronously when possible. Cached or local decisions usually add less than 1 ms, while a Cloud API call typically adds no more than 20–30 ms.
interview.followUp: Why can latency vary? A request may need a remote decision, such as rate-limit tracking in a serverless environment, instead of a local or cached result.

interview.question: Does Arcjet replace network-level DDoS protection?

interview.followUp: How would you handle an application-level abuse pattern? Add an Arcjet rule that matches the needed behavior, run it in dry-run mode when appropriate, and then enforce it in live mode.

interview.question: How does a token bucket rate limit work?
interview.answer: A token bucket limits usage by removing tokens for each request and refilling the bucket at a fixed rate. Capacity sets the largest burst, while refill rate and interval set recovery over time.
interview.followUp: How would you allow bursts but limit sustained traffic? Set capacity above the normal request cost, then choose refill rate and interval for the sustained allowance.

interview.question: How do you apply a Go Guard rate limit?
interview.answer: Guard rules are supplied as GuardRuleInput values in GuardRequest. The request also includes a stable label, and the rule input can include a key and requested token count.
interview.followUp: Why should the key not come from model input? Untrusted input could let callers share or evade buckets; use an authenticated user, session, or API key instead.

interview.question: What is the difference between live and dry-run mode?
interview.answer: ModeLive can block requests, while ModeDryRun records the result without blocking. Go constructors do not silently choose live mode when Mode is empty.
interview.followUp: When is dry-run useful? Use it to observe expected limits and tune settings before enforcing them in production.

IP reputation.explanation: A filter is a rule written in Arcjet's filter language. It matches request values or Arcjet-derived values, such as the user agent, country, VPN status, or proxy status. Non-IP values are checked locally. IP reputation fields need one Cloud API call to supply their data. The filter engine runs inside the SDK's local WebAssembly bundle.

interview.question: What are Arcjet filters and where do they run?
interview.answer: Arcjet filters are application-level rules written in a domain-specific language. They can match literal request fields and derived fields, such as country or VPN status. The filter engine is bundled with the SDK and evaluates expressions locally.
interview.followUp: What causes a network call? Filters that read ip.src.* reputation fields need data from the Arcjet Cloud API; other fields are analyzed locally.

interview.question: How would you block VPN traffic?
interview.answer: A filter can deny traffic when an IP reputation field matches. For example, a rule can deny ip.src.vpn, then the application checks decision.isDenied() and returns an appropriate response.
interview.followUp: How could the application treat one detected service differently? Inspect decision.ip.service after handling other denied rules, then customize the response for that service.

interview.question: What is the performance cost of IP-based filters?
interview.answer: Arcjet makes at most one Cloud API call per request, even when several rules or filters are configured. The SDK uses the closest region, so the usual added time is about 20–30 ms when the call is needed.
interview.followUp: What happens if the API cannot be reached? The SDK normally fails open when an API call is required, but the SDK can be configured to fail closed.

keyPoints: Filters can inspect values that come directly from a request, such as a user-agent header or client IP address.
Filters can also use values Arcjet derives, such as the client's country or whether its IP is linked to a VPN.
The filter engine is included in the SDK's WebAssembly bundle, so parsing and evaluation do not need a network round trip.
IP categories include vpn, proxy, tor, hosting, and relay.
A request uses no more than one Cloud API call, even when it has multiple filters or rules.
A filter can block a particular bot or user-agent value that other protection rules do not recognize.
gotchas: Filters that use IP reputation fields need Cloud API data. This adds network latency.
IP analysis values can be missing. Check availability before using them in application code.
Choose fingerprints that match the fields in your filters. Otherwise, clients may be grouped in an unexpected way.

interview.question: What does ARCJET_BASE_URL control?
interview.answer: ARCJET_BASE_URL is an optional string environment variable. It chooses the URL for the Arcjet Cloud API, whose default is https://decide.arcjet.com.
interview.followUp: When might the default differ? On Fly.io, Arcjet uses https://fly.decide.arcjet.com as the default endpoint.

interview.question: Which SDKs use ARCJET_BASE_URL?
interview.answer: Both the Arcjet JavaScript and Python SDKs read this variable. It should normally remain unset because the documented default is already provided.
interview.followUp: How should production values be stored? Use the secrets-management feature supplied by the hosting platform.

interview.question: When should you set this variable?
interview.answer: Set ARCJET_BASE_URL only when Arcjet Support directs you to. It is not a general application setting that needs changing during ordinary deployment.
interview.followUp: What is the development recommendation? Follow the environment-variable practices of the selected framework, such as using a local environment file during development.

interview.question: How should ASN data be read safely?
interview.answer: Use decision.ip.hasASN() before reading ASN fields such as asnType. The method confirms that all ASN fields are available and narrows their types.
interview.followUp: What does asnType mean? It classifies the network as isp, hosting, business, or education; hosting networks can be more suspicious, but the classification is not proof of abuse.

interview.question: How do you detect anonymized or hosting traffic?
interview.answer: Use decision.ip.isVpn(), isProxy(), isTor(), isRelay(), or isHosting() to test the IP categories. You can also inspect service when it is available to apply a more specific policy.
interview.followUp: How could a policy allow one service? Check hasService() and compare service with a trusted value such as Apple Private Relay before allowing it.

interview.question: How can VPN traffic be blocked?
interview.answer: Create a filter rule with deny: ['ip.src.vpn'] and run it in LIVE mode. After protect(), check decision.isDenied() and return an appropriate response, such as HTTP 403.
interview.followUp: How should missing threat data be handled? Treat absent fields as unknown and avoid assuming that missing data means the IP is safe.

keyPoints: ASN data describes the network operator linked to the client IP.
Use asnType to distinguish common network classes, including hosting and education networks.
Threat categories can include vpn, proxy, tor, hosting, and relay.
Filter rules can use IP analysis to deny traffic before the request continues.
Service information is optional, so keep a policy path for an unknown service.
gotchas: Do not assume every IP field exists. Check availability before using it.
Only trust forwarded client-IP headers when a trusted platform sets them.
IP location is not proof of a user's real location. Avoid using it as the only security signal.

interview.question: How do allow and deny filters differ?
interview.answer: An allow list permits requests that match at least one expression. Requests that match none of the expressions are denied. A deny list blocks matching requests, while non-matching requests are allowed.
interview.followUp: How would you combine country and region checks? Put both conditions in one expression with and, such as ip.src.country eq "US" and ip.src.region eq "California".

interview.question: How can a filter use IP geolocation?
interview.answer: Use fields such as ip.src.country, ip.src.region, and ip.src.vpn in the expression. For example, an allow rule can require a US country and a non-VPN source.
interview.followUp: How can several alternatives be expressed? Use multiple expressions in the list; Arcjet combines them with OR.

interview.question: Where does IP filter data come from?
interview.answer: The IP fields describe the client source IP and require data from Arcjet's IP reputation database. This requires a Cloud API call, while other fields can be analyzed locally.
interview.followUp: Is there one Cloud API call per rule? No. Arcjet makes a single Cloud API call regardless of the rule configuration.

keyPoints: An allow list permits a request when one of its expressions matches.
A deny list blocks a request when one of its expressions matches.
The ip.src.* fields describe the request's source IP address.
Use ip.src.country for a two-letter country code, such as US.
Use ip.src.region for a region value, such as California.
Put conditions joined by and in one expression string.
gotchas: IP location can be wrong, especially for mobile and satellite users. Do not use it as the only security check.
String comparisons are case-sensitive exact matches. Use lower(), upper(), or a case-insensitive regular expression when needed.
A filter cannot define both allow and deny lists.

interview.question: What does the Arcjet IP library do?
interview.answer: The library provides a small utility for finding a request's public IP. It uses platform-specific mechanisms, such as a platform-added header, instead of requiring the main Arcjet SDK.
interview.followUp: Why should the returned IP not be used as trusted identity? The documentation warns that IP values can often be spoofed, particularly through headers.

interview.question: What happens when a request has only private addresses?
interview.answer: It filters out private and internal addresses. When no public address is available after filtering, it returns an empty string.
interview.followUp: What should code do with an empty result? Handle it as an unknown IP rather than assuming that the request is safe.

interview.question: How do you add the utility to a project?
interview.answer: Install the independent package with npm, then pass a Request to the utility. The package does not require the main Arcjet SDK.
interview.followUp: Why might platform-specific handling matter? Hosting platforms can add or overwrite headers that expose the public client IP.

keyPoints: Finding a request's public IP is not always direct.
The utility uses platform-specific ways to locate the address.
One supported platform mechanism is the X-Real-IP header used by Vercel.
You can use this package without installing or configuring the main Arcjet SDK.
The result is empty when every detected address is private or internal.
gotchas: Treat the result as untrusted input. A client can spoof an IP in many situations, especially when the value comes from request headers.
Private and internal addresses are ignored. If a request contains only those addresses, the result is an empty string.

interview.question: How do you inspect inbound IP signals?
interview.answer: Call protect() and inspect decision.ip. Methods such as isHosting(), isVpn(), isProxy(), isTor(), and isAbuser() expose network signals that can guide a custom response.
interview.followUp: How would you handle missing data? Check whether the relevant field or helper reports available data before reading it, because IP analysis may be undefined.

interview.question: When would you use a filter rule?
interview.answer: A filter can deny traffic using fields such as ip.src.vpn. This denial is combined with the other Arcjet rules.
interview.followUp: Can a filter use the threat assessment? No. Inspect decision.ip.threat after protect() instead.

interview.question: Where is the threat assessment stored?
interview.answer: Threat assessment is available only when Arcjet has an assessment. In JavaScript it is decision.ip.threat; in Python it is decision.ip_details.threat; in Go it is decision.IP.Threat.
interview.followUp: What should a public page require before denying? Require at least a medium or high risk level rather than denying on a weak signal alone.

keyPoints: An IP can have several labels, including VPN, proxy, Tor, hosting, or relay.
ASN type describes the network: ISP, hosting, business, or education.
Hosting networks are more likely to contain automated clients, but they can also serve valid APIs.
A privacy relay is different from an open proxy and may represent a legitimate subscribed user.
JavaScript applications read the optional threat assessment from decision.ip.threat.
gotchas: IP fields may be missing unless protect() obtains data from the Arcjet Cloud API.
Do not treat a VPN match alone as proof of abuse.
Blocking privacy relays can also block legitimate clients.
Use the decision after protect() when your policy depends on threat assessment fields.

interview.question: How do you detect a proxy request in Arcjet?
interview.answer: Call `protect()` and then use `decision.ip.isProxy()`. It returns a Boolean that indicates whether the client IP is owned by a proxy provider.
interview.followUp: How can a filter enforce the same policy? Use `ip.src.proxy` in a filter rule and set the rule mode to `LIVE`.

interview.question: What can cause proxy analysis to be unavailable?
interview.answer: The field can be unavailable because IP analysis depends on data from the Arcjet Cloud API. Check the available data before using it.
interview.followUp: What should happen when the field is unavailable? Apply an explicit fallback policy instead of assuming the client is or is not a proxy.

interview.question: Should every proxy request be denied?
interview.answer: A proxy label identifies anonymized network traffic. It does not by itself prove that the request is malicious, so the application should choose a policy appropriate for the route.
interview.followUp: How can you combine this signal with other checks? Inspect other IP signals, such as VPN, Tor, hosting, relay, or threat assessment fields.

keyPoints: `isProxy()` returns `true` when Arcjet identifies the client IP as belonging to a proxy provider.
The method needs IP analysis data from the Arcjet Cloud API, which is obtained when `protect()` calls the API.
Proxy detection can be enforced with a filter or handled in the request code after `protect()`.
Filters can match `ip.src.proxy`, but threat assessment values must be inspected on the decision.
gotchas: IP analysis data may be missing. Check that the field is available before reading related values.

interview.question: What does isRelay() do?
interview.answer: Call protect(), then use decision.ip.isRelay(). It returns true when the client IP belongs to a relay service. You can use the result to customize the response.
interview.followUp: How can you identify a specific relay? Check hasService() first, then compare decision.ip.service with the expected service name.

interview.question: How should relay traffic be treated?
interview.answer: A relay hides the client IP through a relay service. The documentation gives Apple Private Relay as the common example and says its users are less likely to be automated because access requires a paid subscription.
interview.followUp: Should every relay request be denied? No. The documentation warns against denying relay traffic unless blocking those clients is intentional.

interview.question: How can relay detection be used in Arcjet?
interview.answer: Use decision.ip.isRelay() after protect() for application logic. For filter rules, use the source field ip.src.relay instead.
interview.followUp: What happens if IP analysis is unavailable? The related fields may be undefined, so check availability before using them.

interview.question: What does ip.isTor() check?
interview.answer: decision.ip.isTor() returns true when the client IP is known to belong to the Tor network. It is an IP analysis method available after protect() evaluates the request.
interview.followUp: How would you block several anonymized networks? Check isVpn(), isProxy(), and isTor(), or use one filter expression with ip.src.vpn, ip.src.proxy, and ip.src.tor.

interview.question: How would you use ip.isTor() in a request handler?
interview.answer: Call protect(), check whether the decision is already denied, and then call decision.ip.isTor(). Return the response your application policy requires when it returns true.
interview.followUp: How can you allow Apple Private Relay while denying other anonymized traffic? Check the service name first, then deny VPN, proxy, or Tor traffic as appropriate.

interview.question: What is the filter equivalent of ip.isTor()?
interview.answer: The filter field is ip.src.tor. A live filter can deny requests matching that field without custom handler logic.
interview.followUp: What limitation applies to filters and threat assessments? Filters do not read ip.threat, so inspect the decision after protect() for those values.

keyPoints: isTor() returns a boolean that identifies whether the client IP is known to be part of Tor.
The same IP threat intelligence feature covers Tor together with VPN, proxy, hosting, and relay signals.
The method depends on IP analysis data from the Arcjet Cloud API, which is populated when protect() calls the API.
gotchas: IP analysis data may be missing. Check availability before reading optional fields such as the service name or threat assessment.
A filter cannot deny directly from the threat assessment. Inspect the decision after protect() when you need risk, reputation, activity, or entity data.

interview.question: How do you detect a VPN client?
interview.answer: Call protect() and inspect decision.ip.isVpn(). It returns whether the client IP is owned by a VPN provider. You can then customize the response in application code.
interview.followUp: How can VPN traffic be denied before custom handling? Use a filter with the expression ip.src.vpn and set its mode to LIVE.

interview.question: How do you block VPN traffic with Arcjet?
interview.answer: Use a filter rule such as filter({ deny: ["ip.src.vpn"], mode: "LIVE" }). The rule denies requests whose source IP matches Arcjet's VPN signal.
interview.followUp: How would you allow Apple Private Relay but deny other anonymized networks? Inspect the service name after protect(), or use a filter exception for Apple Private Relay.

interview.question: Where is IP threat information available?
interview.answer: The SDK exposes IP analysis on the decision after protect(). In the JavaScript SDK, the VPN check is decision.ip.isVpn(), and detailed threat data is available as decision.ip.threat when Arcjet provides an assessment.
interview.followUp: What should code do when threat data is absent? Check that the field exists before reading it, because responses without an assessment omit it.

interview.answer: In Python, call protect() and then read the geolocation from decision.ip_details. This value can be None, so check it before reading fields such as country.
interview.followUp: What should happen when the country is absent? Use a safe fallback instead of assuming a location or granting location-dependent access.

interview.question: Which geolocation fields are available?
interview.answer: Arcjet can provide latitude, longitude, accuracy radius, timezone, postal code, city, region, country, continent, and related names. Each value may be unavailable.
interview.followUp: How would you make code type-safe? Check ip_details first, then check the specific field before using it.

interview.question: How accurate is IP geolocation?
interview.answer: Geolocation is less dependable for mobile devices, satellite providers, and some ordinary users. City and region are especially error-prone, so these values should not stand alone for security decisions.

interview.question: How is a service name different from an IP category?

interview.question: How do you check an Arcjet decision?
interview.answer: Use isAllowed(), isDenied(), and isErrored() to inspect the overall conclusion. The conclusion represents the highest-severity result from the configured rules.
interview.followUp: Which result wins if one rule returns an error and another denies the request? The overall conclusion is deny because deny has higher severity than error.

interview.question: How do you find why a request was denied?

interview.followUp: How can you inspect findings that did not determine the final conclusion? Iterate over the decision's results property.

interview.question: What does ttl mean on a decision?

interview.followUp: What caching behavior should you account for? The SDK caches deny decisions for the duration of the TTL.

interview.question: What is the difference between `allow` and `deny`?
interview.answer: `allow` names bots that may pass, so detected bots not in the list are denied. `deny` names bots to block, so other detected bots are allowed. The two options cannot be used together.
interview.followUp: How do you block every detected bot? Use `allow: []`; an empty allow list is valid and blocks all detected bots.

interview.question: How does a Next.js route use the bot decision?
interview.answer: Call `aj.protect(req)` and then check `decision.isDenied()` and `decision.reason.isBot()`. A denied bot can receive a 403 response.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect which bots matched? Read the bot reason in each item of `decision.results`, including its `allowed` and `denied` values.

interview.question: When should you use `DRY_RUN`?
interview.answer: `LIVE` enforces the rule and can block requests. `DRY_RUN` records the result without blocking, which is useful for testing a policy.
interview.followUp: What happens if Arcjet cannot process a rule? The rule returns an error result, and the SDK normally fails open; inspect the result message for details.

LIVE.summary: Arcjet Python fixed-window rate limiting counts requests in a fixed time period. Set a maximum count and window length, then deny requests that exceed the limit.
LIVE.explanation: A fixed-window rule counts requests for each client during a set time period. When the count reaches the maximum, a live rule denies later requests until the window ends. The client can identify users with characteristics, such as a user ID, instead of relying only on the request IP.
LIVE.syntax: fixed_window(*, mode: Mode, window: int, max: int, characteristics: Sequence[str] = ()) -> FixedWindow

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: The rule mode. Mode.LIVE can deny requests; Mode.DRY_RUN logs the result without changing the final ALLOW decision.

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: The fixed time window length, in seconds. Python expects an integer.

parameters.name: max
parameters.description: The maximum requests allowed during the window.

parameters.name: characteristics
parameters.description: Optional names of client characteristics used for grouping requests.

LIVE.returns: fixed_window() returns a FixedWindow rule. protect() returns an ArcjetDecision; the async client returns it through a coroutine, while the sync client returns it directly.

example.title: Protect a request with a fixed window
example.code:
import os
from arcjet import Mode, arcjet, fixed_window

aj = arcjet(
    key=os.environ["ARCJET_KEY"],
    rules=[
        fixed_window(
            mode=Mode.LIVE,
            window=60,
            max=10,
        )
    ],
)

def handle(request):
    decision = aj.protect(request)
    if decision.is_denied():
        return {"error": "Too Many Requests"}, 429
    return {"message": "OK"}, 200
example.explanation: This creates one client with a fixed-window rule. It allows 10 requests in 60 seconds, then denies more requests.

interview.question: What is Arcjet rate limiting used for?
interview.answer: Arcjet rate limiting controls how many requests a client can make during a configured period. It can protect APIs, reduce abuse, enforce quotas, and control AI token spend.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from a CDN limit? Arcjet applies the decision inside application code, so the rule can use route, user, plan, or request context.

interview.question: What rate-limit algorithms does Arcjet support?
interview.answer: The fixed-window algorithm counts requests in separate time periods. The sliding-window algorithm uses a moving period to smooth bursts and avoid sharp reset boundaries. Token bucket permits short bursts while maintaining an average rate over time.
interview.followUp: Which algorithm fits bursty traffic? Token bucket is suitable when short bursts should be allowed while a longer-term average is enforced.

interview.question: Where is rate-limit state stored?
interview.answer: Arcjet stores rate-limit state in its Cloud API, so the application does not need infrastructure such as Redis. The state is maintained across multiple application instances.
interview.followUp: What happens after a client exceeds a limit? Arcjet marks the request as over limit until the configured condition resets, and the application decides how to respond.

keyPoints: Use rate limits to enforce per-user AI token budgets and help prevent unexpected spending.
Rules can vary by route, endpoint, or subscription tier.
An over-limit result lets your application block, delay, or otherwise handle the request.

Sliding windows reduce abrupt behavior at time-window boundaries.
Token buckets support bursts by spending tokens and replenishing them over time.

Fixed-window and sliding-window limits can be managed remotely, but token bucket rules require the SDK.
Application rate limiting is not a replacement for protection against large network-level attacks.

interview.question: How can you configure a fixed-window duration?

interview.question: What is Arcjet Shield?
interview.answer: Shield is an application-aware WAF in the Arcjet SDK. It evaluates request metadata over time, combines OWASP Core Rule Set checks with request-pattern analysis, and returns a decision that application code can handle.
interview.followUp: How can it reduce false positives? Configure the fingerprint around the real user identity and apply the decision with route-specific application context instead of using only a network-level block.

interview.question: Where does Shield store tracking state?
interview.answer: Shield keeps state in Arcjet Cloud, so the application does not need to deploy Redis or another tracking service. The state is shared across application instances.
interview.followUp: What is not covered by this design? Large volumetric network attacks should be handled by the hosting provider; Shield focuses on application-level attacks.

interview.question: How does an application enforce a Shield decision?
interview.answer: A route calls the SDK's protect method, checks decision.isDenied(), and then returns the application's response. Use DRY_RUN while testing, and use LIVE when the rule should block.
interview.followUp: How could a sensitive route respond without a plain 403? It could log context, flag the account, require extra verification, or return a route-appropriate structured error.

keyPoints: Shield covers common categories such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting, local and remote file inclusion, code injection, Shellshock, shell injection, and session fixation.
Shield considers repeated behavior, so individually harmless requests can become suspicious when their combined pattern crosses the configured threshold.

interview.question: What does a sliding window rate limit do?

interview.question: What do interval and max configure?

interview.followUp: When could DRY_RUN help? It can show the effect of a proposed limit before enabling blocking.

interview.question: What is a sliding-window rate limit?
interview.answer: A sliding window counts requests over a time interval that moves forward with time. It avoids the sharp reset boundary of a fixed window.
interview.followUp: How is partial usage estimated? Arcjet weights the previous interval by the fraction of that interval that remains, then adds the current interval's requests.

interview.question: What options configure a sliding-window rule?
interview.answer: The required options are `interval`, in seconds, and `max`, the maximum requests allowed during that interval. `mode` controls whether Arcjet blocks requests or only logs results.
interview.followUp: How would you identify clients differently? Set `characteristics` to the client fields used for tracking instead of relying on the default IP-based identity.

interview.question: How does Arcjet calculate remaining capacity?
interview.answer: For a 60-second interval with 50 previous requests, 30 seconds elapsed, and 50 current requests, the estimated usage is 75. With a maximum of 100, 25 requests remain.
interview.followUp: Why is the previous count multiplied by one-half? Thirty of the sixty seconds have elapsed, so half of the previous interval still contributes.

Token bucket.sourceTitle: Rate limiting reference for Node.js | Arcjet Docs
Token bucket.summary: Arcjet token bucket rate limiting limits client requests with a refillable token bucket. Each request spends a chosen number of tokens, and the bucket refills over time.
Token bucket.explanation: A token bucket stores tokens for a client. Each request removes the requested number of tokens. The bucket gains tokens at a fixed rate until it reaches its capacity. When it has too few tokens, the request is denied. The client identity can use the default IP address or configured characteristics.
Token bucket.syntax:
tokenBucket({ mode?, characteristics?, refillRate, interval, capacity })
aj.protect(request, { requested })

parameters.description: Controls enforcement. LIVE blocks denied requests; DRY_RUN logs only.

parameters.description: Tokens added during each interval.

parameters.name: interval
parameters.description: Seconds between token refills.

parameters.name: capacity
parameters.description: Maximum tokens stored in the bucket.

parameters.name: characteristics
parameters.description: Client fields used to identify the rate-limit subject.

parameters.name: requested
parameters.description: Positive integer tokens to remove for this request, passed to protect.

Token bucket.returns: A TokenBucket rule. The protect call returns a decision that can be denied, allowed, or contain an error.

interview.question: How does a token bucket rate limit work?
interview.answer: A token bucket starts with a capacity limit. Requests spend tokens, and refillRate tokens are added every interval until the bucket is full. A request is blocked when it cannot obtain its requested tokens.
interview.followUp: How would you allow bursts but limit long-term traffic? Set capacity for the burst size, then choose refillRate and interval for the sustained rate.

interview.question: What is the difference between LIVE and DRY_RUN?
interview.answer: LIVE mode blocks requests that exceed the rule. DRY_RUN records the result without blocking the request.
interview.followUp: When would you use DRY_RUN? Use it first to observe traffic and tune the limit before enforcing it.

interview.question: How can an application return rate-limit headers?
interview.answer: A decision exposes rate-limit metadata such as max, remaining, window, and reset. The SDK helpers can use this data to write RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy headers.
interview.followUp: What happens with multiple rate-limit results? The tightest remaining budget is advertised; equal max values produce no headers.

keyPoints: Each request spends tokens, and tokens return at a fixed refill rate.
A client cannot continue when the bucket lacks enough tokens for the request.
refillRate sets how many tokens are added during each interval.
capacity sets the largest burst the bucket can store.
characteristics controls the client identity, such as a custom user identifier instead of the default IP address.
gotchas: Token bucket requests need a positive integer requested value. The value says how many tokens the request wants to remove.
Errors normally do not block the request. Check error results and choose whether a sensitive route should fail closed.
The default SDK timeout is 2000 milliseconds, after which processing fails open.
